title: Two-level versus multilevel logic; NAND-only and NOR-only realisations

options: A sum of products (AND gates feeding one OR) or a product of sums: every path is two gates long, so it is the fastest form, though gates may be wide.
A circuit with exactly two gates.
A circuit that uses two supply voltages.
Logic with two outputs.
items.explanation: Two-level trades gate count and fan-in for speed. Multilevel factoring saves gates at the cost of extra delay.

items.prompt: How do you convert an AND-OR circuit into a NAND-only circuit?
options: Replace every AND and the final OR by NAND gates; the two inversions on each internal wire cancel.
Replace only the OR gate by a NAND.
Add an inverter after every AND gate.
It cannot be done without XOR gates.
items.explanation: An OR with inverted inputs is a NAND (De Morgan). Any literal that feeds the output gate directly must be inverted first.

items.prompt: A product-of-sums (OR-AND) circuit converts directly into which single-gate-type form?
options: NOR-NOR
NAND-NAND
NOR-NAND
AND-AND
items.explanation: Mirror image of the SOP rule: OR-AND becomes NOR-NOR.

items.prompt: F = A·B + C·D. How many **2-input NAND** gates does the NAND-only version need?
items.explanation: One NAND for AB, one for CD, and one NAND to combine them: (AB)' NAND (CD)' = AB + CD.

items.prompt: What does **multilevel** logic trade for what?
options: Fewer gates and literals in exchange for more gate delays along the path.
More gates in exchange for less delay.
Fewer inputs in exchange for more outputs.
Nothing: it is always better than two-level.
items.explanation: Factoring shares sub-expressions. Chip designers choose per path, depending on whether that path limits the clock.

items.prompt: Factor F = A·B + A·C to save a gate.
options: A·(B + C)
A + B·C
A·B·C
items.explanation: Two ANDs and an OR become one OR and one AND, with one fewer gate input. The delay is still two levels.

items.prompt: How do you make a NOT gate from a single 2-input NOR?
options: Tie both inputs to the same signal.
Tie one input to 1.
Leave one input floating.
It cannot be done.
items.explanation: NOR(A, A) = (A + A)' = A'. Tying an input to 1 would force the output to 0 forever.

items.prompt: What is the minimum number of 2-input NAND gates needed to build a 2-input **XOR**?
items.explanation: The classic four-NAND XOR: one NAND of A and B, two NANDs mixing each input with that result, and a final NAND. You build it on the bench in this unit's Advanced lab.

options: Any Boolean function can be built from NAND gates only.
A NOR-NOR network implements a product-of-sums expression.
In NAND-NAND form, a single literal that goes straight to the output gate must be inverted first.
A NAND-NAND network implements a product-of-sums expression.
items.explanation: NAND-NAND implements a sum of products; it is NOR-NOR that implements a product of sums.

items.prompt: Why are NAND gates preferred over AND gates in CMOS design?
options: NAND is the natural CMOS gate (series NMOS, parallel PMOS) with four transistors; an AND is a NAND plus an inverter, so it is bigger and slower.
AND gates cannot be built in CMOS.
NAND gates use more power, which keeps them warm.
NAND gates have more inputs.
items.explanation: The same goes for NOR versus OR. Inverting gates come free; non-inverting ones cost an extra stage.
